Here is a mistake that can be a little embarrassing. A student once told her teacher, I'm so boring today. Her teacher smiled and said, no, you're not boring at all. You're bored! What's the difference? Words that end in e-d describe how a person feels: bored, tired, interested, confused. Words that end in i-n-g describe the thing that causes the feeling: a boring meeting, a tiring trip, an interesting book. So if a movie is confusing, you feel confused. If your job is exhausting, you feel exhausted. Here is a simple test. Ask yourself: is this the feeling, or the cause? The feeling ends in e-d. The cause ends in i-n-g. And if you say, I'm interesting, well, that may also be true. But it's a very different sentence.

Hey Vanessa, it's Paulo. I just wanted to tell you about the marathon on Sunday. Honestly, the first ten kilometers were exhausting, and at kilometer thirty I was so frustrated with my legs that I almost stopped. But then I saw my kids holding a sign with my name on it, and I felt so motivated. When I crossed the finish line, I was over the moon, and so relieved it was over. Now I'm a bit fed up with walking, though. My legs hurt every time I take the stairs. Anyway, call me back. I want to hear about your week.

First, I stop and notice how I feel. Then I choose a precise word: not bad, but frustrated. After that, I say what caused it: the meeting was frustrating. Next, I say what I will do about it. In the end, I ask the other person: how about you?
